voice.refText: Twice a week, you sell your plasma, the pale part of your blood. It's the most the law allows. That's the band. A thin strip you wear across your forehead. While you sleep, it lends your brain to a company. And it pays you, by the hour.

Friend.describe: A warm, relaxed male baritone: a man of about thirty who runs a food stall with his best friend. Quick, joking, laughs before his own punchline, a light Singapore English lilt. Close and easy, never loud.

Coffee seller.describe: A dry, brisk female alto: a woman in her fifties who runs the coffee stall next door. Low and a little husky, unimpressed, few words, a faint Singapore English lilt.

Landlord.describe: A smooth, cool male baritone: a landlord in his sixties. Polite, unhurried, quietly cold, every word measured.

Pickpocket.describe: A hoarse, nervous male baritone: a thin man in his thirties. Quick, defensive, a little breathless.

Kid.describe: A high, bright boy's voice, about ten years old. Quick, cheeky, outraged when he loses.

Magician.describe: A bright, theatrical male baritone: a street magician in his forties. Showy and warm, a performer's lift on every word.

Newsreader.describe: A crisp, bright female alto: a television newsreader in her thirties. Polished and quick, a smile in the voice, every line a headline.

Coach.describe: A loud, upbeat male baritone: a street salesman in his forties. Bouncy and confident, a pitch voice, every line a slogan.

lines.text: Friend: Trust me?
lines.say: Trust me?
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: Friend: Half?
lines.say: [baffled, delighted, half a laugh, looking at the board] Half?
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: Coffee seller: Half.
lines.say: [flat, bored, already stacking cups, not looking up] Half.
lines.speaker: Coffee seller

lines.text: So what if an AI predicted every choice you make, and your life got cheaper every time you did what it predicted?
lines.say: [leaning in, mischievous, a grin on the last clause, as if offering a deal] So what if an AI predicted every choice you make, and your life got cheaper every time you did what it predicted?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: That card over your head is your tag: what you'll do next. Do it, and your rent can fall to half. Don't, and your tag goes red where everyone can see it, and your prices climb.
lines.say: [brisk, a dealer laying out terms, bright on the halving, a shade colder and slower on crimson] what you'll do next. Do it, and your rent can fall to half. Don't, and your tag goes red where everyone can see it, and your prices climb.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Closing time. A food court in Singapore. You and your best friend run this stall. Every night you count the cash box. Every night he holds out his hand for the key, like he's going to run off with the money. Every night you hold it over his palm, and pocket it. The oldest joke you two have. Tonight the joke came with a number.
lines.say: [warm, close, the place in two breaths, then a rhythm like a habit, the last sentence dropped quiet with a smile] Closing time. A food court in Singapore. You and your best friend run this stall. Every night you count the cash box. Every night he holds out his hand for the key, like he's going to run off with the money. Every night you hold it over his palm, and pocket it. The oldest joke you two have. Tonight the joke came with a number.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And here's the thing. It's right ninety-nine times in a hundred. About everybody.
lines.say: [a secret shared, relish on the number, the last two words hushed as a hook] And here's the thing. It's right ninety-nine times in a hundred. About everybody.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Here's how it works. Over every head, a tag: what you'll do in the next ten seconds, and how sure it is. The city watches from every lamppost.
lines.say: [clear, exact, the rule said once, a glance upward on the last line] Here's how it works. Over every head, a tag: what you'll do in the next ten seconds, and how sure it is. The city watches from every lamppost.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Under each lamp, a board with your rate. A hundred is full price. Fifty is half. Do what your tag says, and your rate drops. Your coffee, your fare, your rent, all cheaper. It knows you. Ninety-nine times in a hundred, it knows you.
lines.say: [plain, each item a small gift, then slower and almost fond on the last sentence] Under each lamp, a board with your rate. A hundred is full price. Fifty is half. Do what your tag says, and your rate drops. Your coffee, your fare, your rent, all cheaper. It knows you. Ninety-nine times in a hundred, it knows you.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Go against your tag, and it turns red, and your rate climbs. Red means trouble, and everyone can see it. One more thing. It only knows the choices you've already made. It has never seen you do something new. Remember that.
lines.say: [measured, a warning without heat, each limit its own beat, the last two words almost a whisper and a little playful] Go against your tag, and it turns red, and your rate climbs. Red means trouble, and everyone can see it. One more thing. It only knows the choices you've already made. It has never seen you do something new. Remember that.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Friend: Oh, come on.
lines.say: [outraged, laughing, the torn card still in his hand] Oh, come on.
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: Tear it off, and the next lamp prints another. It saw that coming too.
lines.say: [dry, amused, the second sentence a shrug] Tear it off, and the next lamp prints another. It saw that coming too.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: He hums all the way home. He stops. It saw that too.
lines.say: [amused, fond, the last sentence dry] He hums all the way home. He stops. It saw that too.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Friend: It likes me.
lines.say: [delighted, walking backwards, arms out, loud] It likes me.
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: Nobody here finds a price on a choice strange. This city has billed drivers for its busiest roads by time of day since 1998.
lines.say: [dry, matter of fact, a shrug in the voice] Nobody here finds a price on a choice strange. This city has billed drivers for its busiest roads by time of day since nineteen ninety-eight.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Your rate starts at a hundred. Tomorrow you'll find out which way it moves.
lines.say: [quiet, a hook, a half-smile] Your rate starts at a hundred. Tomorrow you'll find out which way it moves.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Morning. You've worked it out. It guesses. So guess wrong.
lines.say: [brisk, confident, mischievous, a dare on the last three words] Morning. You've worked it out. It guesses. So guess wrong.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You beat it four times. Four reds, and every red costs you. Your rate's up a quarter, before breakfast. And on the fifth try, it's caught up.
lines.say: [deadpan, the joke landing dry, a wince on the number] You beat it four times. Four reds, and every red costs you. Your rate's up a quarter, before breakfast. And on the fifth try, it's caught up.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: A professor once wrote a tiny program that guessed which of two keys people would press when they tried to type at random. Right seventy to eighty per cent of the time. He couldn't beat it himself.
lines.say: [calm, a story told at a table, a grin held back on the last sentence] A professor once wrote a tiny program that guessed which of two keys people would press when they tried to type at random. Right seventy to eighty per cent of the time. He couldn't beat it himself.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Trying to be random is a pattern.
lines.say: [flat, the landing line, a complete thought] Trying to be random is a pattern.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So your coffee this morning costs more than it did last night.
lines.say: [dry, sympathetic, a smile at your expense] So your coffee this morning costs more than it did last night.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Coffee seller: You're up today.
lines.say: [dry, eyebrows up, tapping the board, enjoying it] You're up today.
lines.speaker: Coffee seller

lines.text: Fine. Let a coin choose.
lines.say: [quick, a new plan, cheerful] Fine. Let a coin choose.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Friend: It's in my head.
lines.say: [spooked, half laughing, wiping his hand, the laugh not quite working] It's in my head.
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: A coin is random. Reaching for it isn't. The tag doesn't guess the coin. It guesses him, reaching for it again.
lines.say: [level, three short blows, the last one quiet and pleased with itself] A coin is random. Reaching for it isn't. The tag doesn't guess the coin. It guesses him, reaching for it again.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Problem one. Fighting your tag costs money, and it learns how you fight. So you stop fighting yours. And start reading everyone else's.
lines.say: [leaning in, numbering the trouble, then a turn, brightening, a scheme forming on the last sentence] Problem one. Fighting your tag costs money, and it learns how you fight. So you stop fighting yours. And start reading everyone else's.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lunch. You read the tags over the queue, and serve each plate before they ask.
lines.say: [quick, sly, a card sharp at work] Lunch. You read the tags over the queue, and serve each plate before they ask.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Coffee seller: Show-off.
lines.say: [muttered, mouth still open, impressed against her will] Show-off.
lines.speaker: Coffee seller

lines.text: Nobody waits. Their tags come true, yours comes true, and your rate drops. The queue doubles by the weekend, and the court next door starts reading tags too.
lines.say: [brisk, triumphant, a montage in one breath, the last clause a raised eyebrow] Nobody waits. Their tags come true, yours comes true, and your rate drops. The queue doubles by the weekend, and the court next door starts reading tags too.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The landlord's letter. A low rate means low rent.
lines.say: [quick, a held breath] The landlord's letter. A low rate means low rent.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Landlord: Keep it up.
lines.say: [clipped, approving, a man who approves of very little] Keep it up.
lines.speaker: Landlord

lines.text: Friend: Half!
lines.say: [a shout of joy, hand already up] Half!
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: Half rent on the stall. And a thought you can't put down. If you can read your customers' tags, you can read anyone's.
lines.say: [warm, then slower, a grin spreading, the last sentence a dare to yourself] Half rent on the stall. And a thought you can't put down. If you can read your customers' tags, you can read anyone's.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The platform. A hood behind a woman's bag, and a red tag: takes wallet. The first time the city has forecast a crime.
lines.say: [hushed, quick, a change of air, the last word slow] The platform. A hood behind a woman's bag, and a red tag: takes wallet. The first time the city has forecast a crime.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Pickpocket: I didn't touch it.
lines.say: [frightened, fast, hands open, to a platform of faces] I didn't touch it.
lines.speaker: Pickpocket

lines.text: Call the police? He hasn't done anything yet. A forecast isn't a crime.
lines.say: [the viewer's question said back, then dry and exact, a shrug on the last sentence] Call the police? He hasn't done anything yet. A forecast isn't a crime.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Every head turns anyway. Doors shut on him. The coffee seller won't pour. A red tag is a verdict everyone can read, and nobody asks for the trial. By the weekend he's afraid to move at all. His tag says stands still. Safest man on the platform.
lines.say: [cold and quick on the first three sentences, level on the verdict, then dry and amused on the ending] Every head turns anyway. Doors shut on him. The coffee seller won't pour. A red tag is a verdict everyone can read, and nobody asks for the trial. By the weekend he's afraid to move at all. His tag says stands still. Safest man on the platform.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The kid with the cap plays rock-paper-scissors for the seat by the door. Wins with rock. His tag says rock again. So the man beside him throws paper, every time.
lines.say: [amused, quick, a commentator at a small match, the last three words a punchline] The kid with the cap plays rock-paper-scissors for the seat by the door. Wins with rock. His tag says rock again. So the man beside him throws paper, every time.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Kid: No fair.
lines.say: [outraged, seven years old, cap in hand] No fair.
lines.speaker: Kid

lines.text: People who win tend to play the same thing again.
lines.say: [clear, calm, the fact plain, a smile under it] People who win tend to play the same thing again.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Magician: Pick a card.
lines.say: [showman's patter, bright, already fading as the crowd leaves] Pick a card.
lines.speaker: Magician

lines.text: His tag says where the queen is hiding. Nobody stays for a trick they've already seen. By lunch, no act.
lines.say: [deadpan, two short blows, the second softer] His tag says where the queen is hiding. Nobody stays for a trick they've already seen. By lunch, no act.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Now the whole city is reading tags. The penalty kick. Tag says left, keeper goes left.
lines.say: [building like a commentator, gleeful, the save landing like a goal] Now the whole city is reading tags. The penalty kick. Tag says left, keeper goes left.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Bet on it? Everyone can read the tag, so everyone bets the same way. The bookie read it first, and pays back only what you put in.
lines.say: [the viewer's idea said back with a grin, then dry, the last clause flat as a shut window] Bet on it? Everyone can read the tag, so everyone bets the same way. The bookie read it first, and pays back only what you put in.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Kick against your tag and your rate climbs, so every striker obeys. Every keeper reads it. Nobody scores.
lines.say: [quick, then flat on the last three words] Kick against your tag and your rate climbs, so every striker obeys. Every keeper reads it. Nobody scores.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Newsreader: Another nil-nil.
lines.say: [broadcast even, squared off, the smallest sigh in it] Another nil-nil.
lines.speaker: Newsreader

lines.text: Phone records from fifty thousand people once showed this. Where a person will be is, in principle, guessable up to about ninety-three per cent of the time.
lines.say: [calm, exact, a touch of awe held back on the number] Phone records from fifty thousand people once showed this. Where a person will be is, in principle, guessable up to about ninety-three per cent of the time.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You thought you were a free spirit. You're a timetable.
lines.say: [dry, warm, the joke on you] You thought you were a free spirit. You're a timetable.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The morning train. Forty heads. Forty tags, the same three words. Nobody looks out of the window.
lines.say: [hushed, slow, awed, the last sentence a little eerie] The morning train. Forty heads. Forty tags, the same three words. Nobody looks out of the window.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: To live cheap here, you have to be easy to guess. So here's problem two: the cheapest people in this city never surprise anyone.
lines.say: [leaning in, low, the number plain, the last four words a chill with a smile in it] To live cheap here, you have to be easy to guess. So here's problem two: the cheapest people in this city never surprise anyone.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The man with the same lunch. Same table, same minute, same dish, for a year. Lowest rate in the city.
lines.say: [dry, a rhythm like a clock, the last sentence flat and mock-admiring] The man with the same lunch. Same table, same minute, same dish, for a year. Lowest rate in the city.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Friend: That's the champion?
lines.say: [incredulous, leaning over the counter, a laugh in it] That's the champion?
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: People farm it. In 1902, Hanoi paid a bounty for every rat tail. Officials found people breeding rats for the tails. Pay for predictability, and people breed it.
lines.say: [amused, a story with a sting, a chuckle on the breeding, the last sentence slow and exact] People farm it. In nineteen oh two, Hanoi paid a bounty for every rat tail. Officials found people breeding rats for the tails. Pay for predictability, and people breed it.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: On the street, a man sells boring.
lines.say: [deadpan, a smile in it] On the street, a man sells boring.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Coach: Same route. Same lunch. Same face.
lines.say: [a street seller's chant, upbeat, selling it] Same route. Same lunch. Same face.
lines.speaker: Coach

lines.text: Your rate falls. Sixty-one. Fifty-five. You've learned to read your tag before you reach.
lines.say: [pleased on the numbers, dropping like coins, then the last sentence slower, a first flicker of unease under the smile] Your rate falls. Sixty-one. Fifty-five. You've learned to read your tag before you reach.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Quiet all week. Then tonight, the landlord impression. The napkin tie.
lines.say: [warm, relieved, a laugh already starting] Quiet all week. Then tonight, the landlord impression. The napkin tie.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Friend: It knows the bit.
lines.say: [deflated, a rueful laugh, pulling the napkin off] It knows the bit.
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: He stops doing his bits. What's a joke when the tag says it first? That's what the discount really costs. Not money. Surprises.
lines.say: [low, level, the point landing, no pity in it] He stops doing his bits. What's a joke when the tag says it first? That's what the discount really costs. Not money. Surprises.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And the city's board, how often the tags come true, says ninety-nine point five now. Every week it's right more often. Is it getting smarter? Hold that thought.
lines.say: [quiet, a hook, the last three words slower and colder] And the city's board, how often the tags come true, says ninety-nine point five now. Every week it's right more often. Is it getting smarter? Hold that thought.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You thought it read minds. Nothing reads minds.
lines.say: [plain, a correction said with a grin] You thought it read minds. Nothing reads minds.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: In 2008, brain scans could guess whether a person would press a left or a right button a few seconds before they felt they'd chosen. The guess was right about sixty per cent of the time. A coin gets fifty.
lines.say: [clear, careful, a story told exactly, the last sentence dry as a shrug] In two thousand and eight, brain scans could guess whether a person would press a left or a right button a few seconds before they felt they'd chosen. The guess was right about sixty per cent of the time. A coin gets fifty.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Sixty. And the tag over you says ninety-nine. So where does the rest come from? Keep that question. We'll answer it.
lines.say: [slow, puzzled, the question held open like a riddle, not answered] Sixty. And the tag over you says ninety-nine. So where does the rest come from? Keep that question. We'll answer it.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And your best friend never stopped fighting his tag. The coin. The torn tags. The jokes he wouldn't drop. Every red cost him. His rate climbs, and his rent with it. He's been staring at the cash box all week.
lines.say: [low, watching, the two Ups like steps, the last sentence quiet and uneasy] And your best friend never stopped fighting his tag. The coin. The torn tags. The jokes he wouldn't drop. Every red cost him. His rate climbs, and his rent with it. He's been staring at the cash box all week.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Friend: Machine hates me.
lines.say: [grumbling, half a joke, not looking up from the box] Machine hates me.
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: Tomorrow his hand comes out for the key, like every night. And this time the tag won't think it's a joke.
lines.say: [low, a dread building under a plain voice, the last five words slow] Tomorrow his hand comes out for the key, like every night. And this time the tag won't think it's a joke.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Closing. The court half dark. His hand comes out.
lines.say: [hushed, short, the breath held] Closing. The court half dark. His hand comes out.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Friend: Trust me?
lines.say: Trust me?
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: Friend: Machine's drunk.
lines.say: [a laugh that starts and stops halfway, shaken] Machine's drunk.
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: His tag says he'll take the key, for real. Seventy-one per cent sure. You've put that key in your pocket a thousand times as a joke. Tonight it's the first time you've locked something away from him.
lines.say: [low, slow, the sting felt, the landing line finished] His tag says he'll take the key, for real. Seventy-one per cent sure. You've put that key in your pocket a thousand times as a joke. Tonight it's the first time you've locked something away from him.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Coffee seller: Not with that tag.
lines.say: [firm, not cruel, eyes on the card not the man] Not with that tag.
lines.speaker: Coffee seller

lines.text: His coffee's gone. His rent doubles. And the whole platform would rather sit next to the pickpocket.
lines.say: [brisk, each blow quicker, a grin breaking on the last clause] His coffee's gone. His rent doubles. And the whole platform would rather sit next to the pickpocket.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Pickpocket: Plenty of room, everyone.
lines.say: [sly, cheerful, a host welcoming guests] Plenty of room, everyone.
lines.speaker: Pickpocket

lines.text: But the tag doesn't say thief. It says seventy-one. So who gets a red tag like that?
lines.say: [leaning in, low, a hook, the number said twice with weight] But the tag doesn't say thief. It says seventy-one. So who gets a red tag like that?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: In America, a risk score used in courts wrongly flagged Black defendants as future criminals at almost twice the rate of white defendants.
lines.say: [level, serious, exact, no heat] In America, a risk score used in courts wrongly flagged Black defendants as future criminals at almost twice the rate of white defendants.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And a crowd of strangers online, given two lines about each defendant, predicted who'd reoffend about as well as the software did.
lines.say: [calm, a shade of disbelief, slower on the last clause] And a crowd of strangers online, given two lines about each defendant, predicted who'd reoffend about as well as the software did.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: He's broke, and his rent just doubled. That's all the machine sees: a broke man next to a cash box. It isn't seeing a thief. It's seeing a man in trouble. And it can't tell the two apart. Neither can the food court.
lines.say: [quiet, level, the landing line complete, the last sentence dry and a little bitter] He's broke, and his rent just doubled. That's all the machine sees: a broke man next to a cash box. It isn't seeing a thief. It's seeing a man in trouble. And it can't tell the two apart. Neither can the food court.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Every night his number climbs. Seventy-one. Eighty. Eighty-eight. Tonight your tag says count the box, alone. You don't.
lines.say: [the numbers like footsteps, then a beat, the last sentence quiet and decided] Every night his number climbs. Seventy-one. Eighty. Eighty-eight. Tonight your tag says count the box, alone. You don't.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Friend: That cost you.
lines.say: [soft, surprised, a grin breaking through, looking at your card] That cost you.
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: Rent's due tomorrow. Both your rents, in one tin box. And that's when his tag says the thing the whole court has been waiting for.
lines.say: [low, steady, the stakes counted, then a held breath and a hook] Rent's due tomorrow. Both your rents, in one tin box. And that's when his tag says the thing the whole court has been waiting for.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Closing. The last customers gone. The coffee seller's phone is already up. Because his tag says takes the box. Ninety-four.
lines.say: [quiet, tight, each sentence shorter, the number alone and cold] Closing. The last customers gone. The coffee seller's phone is already up. Because his tag says takes the box. Ninety-four.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Everything it ever got right about you was small. A coffee, a train, a key. When scientists watched people make a choice that mattered, where real charity money went, the early brain signal they used to predict small choices was missing.
lines.say: [low, thinking aloud, then careful and exact on the fact, a spark on missing] Everything it ever got right about you was small. A coffee, a train, a key. When scientists watched people make a choice that mattered, where real charity money went, the early brain signal they used to predict small choices was missing.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: It has never seen you choose something that mattered. And you're about to.
lines.say: [slow, intimate, the last four words a dare] It has never seen you choose something that mattered. And you're about to.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: A month of half price. What did you stop doing for it?
lines.say: [quiet, a question to you and nobody else, no answer offered] A month of half price. What did you stop doing for it?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Pocket the key, and your tag comes true, and your rent stays half. His tag says he'll take the box. So what if you just give it to him? Hand him the key, and your tag goes red in front of everyone. And your rent goes back to full.
lines.say: [level, two doors held open, no lean either way, the last clause slower] Pocket the key, and your tag comes true, and your rent stays half. His tag says he'll take the box. So what if you just give it to him? Hand him the key, and your tag goes red in front of everyone. And your rent goes back to full.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Remember? It only knows what you've done before. So do something you've never done.
lines.say: [a grin in the voice, the plant called back, then quick and bright, a starting gun on the last three words] Remember? It only knows what you've done before. So do something you've never done.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Ninety-four.
lines.say: [one word, very quiet, then nothing] Ninety-four.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The first blank card the city has ever made. His tag said he'd steal the box. Now it says nothing.
lines.say: [hushed, awed, slow, a smile arriving at the end] The first blank card the city has ever made. His tag said he'd steal the box. Now it says nothing.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Friend: I was going to.
lines.say: [barely out, eyes on the key, honest] I was going to.
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: Kid: Do it again.
lines.say: [a shout from the back, thrilled, standing on his chair] Do it again.
lines.speaker: Kid

lines.text: You can't steal what you've just been handed. And the machine had no card for that.
lines.say: [warm, certain, triumphant under a quiet voice, the landing line complete] You can't steal what you've just been handed. And the machine had no card for that.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Two red tags. You broke yours, and he did the opposite of his. Every face in the court turned toward them. And on the pillar, for the first time, the city's board flaps down.
lines.say: [slow, wide, a held picture, then a lift of wonder on the last clause] you broke yours, and he did the opposite of his. Every face in the court turned toward them. And on the pillar, for the first time, the city's board flaps down.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: It knows you. Ninety-nine times in a hundred, it knows you. That's what everyone thought. But it was never reading you. You were reading it, and doing what it said.
lines.say: [the planted line said back soft, a hard stop on the No, then slow and clear, a reveal] It knows you. Ninety-nine times in a hundred, it knows you. That's what everyone thought. But it was never reading you. You were reading it, and doing what it said.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Drivers tracked by their insurer for a discount braked hard about a fifth less often. Within six months. The watching changed the driving.
lines.say: [clear, exact, the second sentence a beat on its own, the third slow and pointed] Drivers tracked by their insurer for a discount braked hard about a fifth less often. Within six months. The watching changed the driving.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: An economist put it in 1975: lean on a number to control people, and the number stops behaving.
lines.say: [dry, a rule from an old book, the last four words slow] An economist put it in nineteen seventy-five: lean on a number to control people, and the number stops behaving.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Run the board backwards. Ninety-nine. Ninety-three. Eighty-four. Seventy-one. The night it started, it was right seven times in ten. It didn't get smarter. You got easier to guess, because being easy to guess made you cheaper. That's where the rest came from. You.
lines.say: [a dare, the numbers falling like a countdown, the last sentence flat and delighted] Run the board backwards. Ninety-nine. Ninety-three. Eighty-four. Seventy-one. The night it started, it was right seven times in ten. It didn't get smarter. You got easier to guess, because being easy to guess made you cheaper. That's where the rest came from. You.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: A hundred and sixty teams once tried to predict how children's lives would turn out. Thousands of facts on every family. The best guesses were only slightly better than a simple one from four facts. People are hard to predict. Unless they're paid to be.
lines.say: [calm, a story told exactly, a shade of wonder on the last clause] A hundred and sixty teams once tried to predict how children's lives would turn out. Thousands of facts on every family. The best guesses were only slightly better than a simple one from four facts. People are hard to predict. Unless they're paid to be.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: It never got better at seeing you. You got better at being seen.
lines.say: [intimate, slower, the heart of it, finished] It never got better at seeing you. You got better at being seen.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: A sociologist named it in 1948: a false belief can make itself true, and the prophet points to what happened as proof he was right all along. Predicting a comet, he noted, doesn't change its orbit.
lines.say: [dry, a story from an old journal, a small smile on the comet] A sociologist named it in nineteen forty-eight: a false belief can make itself true, and the prophet points to what happened as proof he was right all along. Predicting a comet, he noted, doesn't change its orbit.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Predicting a comet doesn't move the comet. Predicting a person does.
lines.say: [slow, clear, the landing line, a beat before the last word] Predicting a comet doesn't move the comet. Predicting a person does.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: A city of teal lights. Under every one, someone doing what the card says. And one lamp that just got dimmer.
lines.say: [hushed, wide, awed, the last sentence a quiet grin] A city of teal lights. Under every one, someone doing what the card says. And one lamp that just got dimmer.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Newsreader: A blank forecast, filmed at a food court.
lines.say: [broadcast even, crisp, a flicker of disbelief on blank] A blank forecast, filmed at a food court.
lines.speaker: Newsreader

lines.text: By breakfast, everyone's copying you. Hand over a key, and save half.
lines.say: [light, amused, a grin spreading, quick on the last three words] By breakfast, everyone's copying you. Hand over a key, and save half.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Friend: That was ours.
lines.say: [affronted, arms folded, mock-wounded] That was ours.
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: By lunch the tags predict that too: hands over key. It watched a thousand people do it. Your surprise is just another habit now.
lines.say: [dry, a shrug, the second sentence a wry aside] hands over key. It watched a thousand people do it. Your surprise is just another habit now.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Newsreader: Confidence is back to ninety-nine.
lines.say: [broadcast even, brisk, relieved on behalf of the city] Confidence is back to ninety-nine.
lines.speaker: Newsreader

lines.text: Landlord: Full rent.
lines.say: [clipped, a hint of respect he'd never admit] Full rent.
lines.speaker: Landlord

lines.text: Your tags stay red. Red means full price.
lines.say: [dry, matter of fact, proud] Your tags stay red. Red means full price.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Coffee seller: Full price. Same?
lines.say: [dry, a small warmth, the cup already moving] Full price. Same?
lines.speaker: Coffee seller

lines.text: The train. Two red tags in the middle, paying full fare, and every head sneaking a look.
lines.say: [amused, sly, the last clause a stage whisper] The train. Two red tags in the middle, paying full fare, and every head sneaking a look.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Friend: Trust me?
lines.say: [bright, easy, the oldest joke, grinning before the words; the same read each time it comes back, at the crimson seventy-one and on the train, so the card and the faces do the changing] Trust me?
lines.speaker: Friend

lines.text: You never look up.
lines.say: [quiet, warm, complete] You never look up.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Except one. The kid with the cap. Nothing on his card. Whatever he does next, the machine can't guess it. And the city hasn't noticed yet.
lines.say: [soft, delighted, a secret shared, the last word held] Except one. The kid with the cap. Nothing on his card. Whatever he does next, the machine can't guess it. And the city hasn't noticed yet.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So, would you pay full price to make your card go blank? Tell us in the comments. And if you would, hit like and subscribe.
lines.say: [warm, direct, a friend daring you with a grin, brisk on the last clause] So, would you pay full price to make your card go blank? Tell us in the comments. And if you would, hit like and subscribe.
lines.speaker: narrator
